newsitem.title: USA: CVS to buy Revco for $2.8 billion. [CORRECTED 10:04 GMT 08/02]
newsitem.headline: CVS to buy Revco for $2.8 billion. [CORRECTED 10:04 GMT 08/02]

text.p: CVS Corp., the nation's fifth-largest chain of drug stores, said Friday it will acquire rival Revco D.S. Inc. for $2.8 billion in stock, creating the nation's second-largest drug store chain.

The combined company, which will dominate the eastern half of the country, will have about 4,000 stores and annual sales of $13 billion, making it the largest in terms of outlets and second-largest behind Walgreen Co. in terms of total sales.

While the announcement did not state how many jobs may be eliminated in the merger, sources familiar with the companies said that most of the 1,000 people employed at Revco's Ohio headquarters were likely to lose their jobs.

CVS said the new company, which will retain the name CVS, will be led by its existing senior management and retain the CVS headquarters in Woonsocket, R.I. Revco's headquarters in Twinsburg, Ohio, will be phased out.
The company said the only layoffs it anticipated would be in connection with the phase-out of Revco's headquarters, but it did not offer any numbers.
Revco declined to comment on expected job losses, except to say that Chief Executive Dwayne Hoven would not remain with the new company after the merger is completed.
"He will stay through the transition. He is intently interested in seeing to it that his people in Twinsburg are well taken care of," a Revco spokeswoman said.

The transaction will solidify CVS's position in the sector and allow it to expand significantly. Analysts said the companies have little geographic overlap and the combination is not expected to generate significant antitrust concerns.
CVS stores are located primarily in the Northeast and Middle Atlantic regions while Revco stores are mostly in Midwest and Southeast.
The merger calls for CVS to pay the equivalent of $40.64 in its shares for each share of Revco, based on Thursday's closing stock prices. CVS also will assume $900 million of Revco debt.
CVS stock closed Thursday at $44 a share and Revco at $38, both on the New York Stock Exchange, but enthusiastic investors pushed both higher Friday.
Revco added $3.375 to $41.375 in heavy trading while CVS gained $3.125 to $47.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It's a great deal for CVS. The structure (of the deal) is going to allow it to be additive to earnings immediately," Eric Bosshard of Midwest Research-Maxus Group said.
"(CVS and Revco) are the two most dominant market share players in the industry and market share is really the name of the game."
Both companies acknowledged last month that they were discussing a combination of their businesses.

Two shareholders likely to prosper from the merger are Revco CEO Hoven and Revco co-Chairman Sam Zell. Zell's Chilmark Fund LP holds a 19.2 percent stake in Revco and Hoven also has large holdings in the company.
CVS said the new company plans to open or relocate 300 stores a year after the merger is completed.

Analysts said the CVS-Revco union likely marks at least a near-term end to big mergers in the industry, although dozens of small chains still exist and are expected to get scooped up or join forces with bigger operators.

Revco had agreed in November, 1995, to merge with Rite Aid Corp. in a $1.8 billion deal, but that merger was blocked by on anti-trust grounds, (corrects to show that Revco-Rite Aid deal was not hostile).

"A number of companies in the sector are coming to us and asking us what they should do strategically," said Marty Murrer, managing director at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, which advised CVS in the Revco deal and has been a key player in the sector's biggest transactions.
Arbor Drug Inc., Genovese Drug Stores Inc. and privately held Duane Reade Inc. have been cited as likely candidates to participate in the consolidation sweeping the sector.

The proposed friendly union between Revco and Rite Aid collapsed last April after state and federal regulators contended a combination would create antitrust issues and potentially drive up consumer prices.
